title: Burgundy's 33 Grands Crus: A Systematic Study
description: A complete overview of all 33 Grands Crus — their location, character and place in Burgundy's hierarchy.
lessons.0.title: Understanding Grand Cru in Burgundy
lessons.0.slides.0.title: Understanding Grand Cru in Burgundy
lessons.0.slides.0.subtitle: 12 minutes
lessons.0.slides.0.description: What Grand Cru means in Burgundy, why there are only 33, and how they differ from Grands Crus in other wine regions.
lessons.0.slides.1.title: Grand Cru: The Pinnacle of Terroir
lessons.0.slides.1.content: Burgundy's 33 Grands Crus represent just over 1% of total production, yet they define the world's most precise quality hierarchy. Unlike Bordeaux's Grands Crus Classés (estate-based), Burgundy's Grands Crus are defined by vineyard parcel, not by producer.
lessons.0.slides.1.keyPoints.0: 33 Grands Crus total — certified by AOC as the finest vineyard parcels
lessons.0.slides.1.keyPoints.1: Labelled by vineyard name only — the producer's name appears below the vineyard name
lessons.0.slides.1.keyPoints.2: Land area: total Grand Cru area is approximately 566 ha (vs 27,000 ha for regional Bourgogne)
lessons.0.slides.1.keyPoints.3: Price range: from €100–150 per bottle for some (Corton, Échézeaux) to €15,000–50,000+ for Romanée-Conti
lessons.0.slides.2.title: Grand Cru vs Premier Cru: The Key Differences
lessons.0.slides.2.content: Both are elite appellations, but Grands Crus stand alone as the apex of Burgundy's quality hierarchy.
lessons.0.slides.2.keyPoints.0: Grand Cru: labelled by vineyard name only (e.g. 'Chambertin Grand Cru'); no village name required
lessons.0.slides.2.keyPoints.1: Premier Cru: labelled as 'Village Name + 1er Cru + Vineyard Name' (e.g. 'Gevrey-Chambertin 1er Cru Clos Saint-Jacques')
lessons.0.slides.2.keyPoints.2: Grand Cru yield limits: 35–37 hl/ha (strictest in Burgundy)
lessons.0.slides.2.keyPoints.3: Grand Cru minimum alcohol: slightly higher requirement — 11.5% for reds, 12% for whites
lessons.0.slides.3.title: Distribution of the 33 Grands Crus
lessons.0.slides.3.content: The 33 Grands Crus are concentrated in three zones: Chablis (7), the Côte de Nuits (24) and the Côte de Beaune (8, including 1 shared).
lessons.0.slides.3.keyPoints.0: Chablis: 7 Grands Crus — all white (Chardonnay), approximately 100 ha total
lessons.0.slides.3.keyPoints.1: Côte de Nuits: 24 Grands Crus — predominantly red (Pinot Noir); only Musigny produces Grand Cru white
lessons.0.slides.3.keyPoints.2: Côte de Beaune: 8 Grands Crus — red (Corton) and white (Corton-Charlemagne, Montrachet family)
lessons.0.slides.3.keyPoints.3: None in: Côte Chalonnaise, Mâconnais or Beaujolais
lessons.0.slides.4.title: 💡 Key Take-aways
lessons.0.slides.4.points.0: 🍷 Grand Cru in Burgundy is about the vineyard, not the producer — the same Grand Cru can vary enormously by estate
lessons.0.slides.4.points.1: 🍷 There are just 33 Grands Crus covering ~566 ha — extreme rarity drives extreme prices
lessons.0.slides.4.points.2: 🍷 24 of 33 Grands Crus are in the Côte de Nuits — the heartland of red Grand Cru Burgundy
lessons.0.slides.4.points.3: 🍷 The strictest yields in Burgundy (35–37 hl/ha) apply to Grand Cru vineyards
lessons.0.slides.5.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.0.question: How many Grands Crus does Burgundy have in total?
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.0.explanati: Burgundy has exactly 33 Grands Crus, covering approximately 566 ha and representing about 1% of total production. This compares with approximately 640 Premier Cru vineyards and 44 Village appellations below them.
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.1.question: How is a Burgundy Grand Cru labelled?
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.1.options.0: A. By the estate name only
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.1.options.1: B. By the village name followed by the vineyard name
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.1.options.2: C. By the vineyard name alone — no village name is required
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.1.options.3: D. By the grape variety and the vintage year only
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.1.explanati: A Burgundy Grand Cru is labelled by the vineyard (parcel) name alone — for example 'Chambertin Grand Cru' — without needing to mention the village (Gevrey-Chambertin). This contrasts with Premier Cru, which always includes the village name.
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.2.question: What are the maximum permitted yields for Grand Cru vineyards?
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.2.options.0: A. 55 hl/ha (the same as Village level)
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.2.options.3: D. No yield limits apply to Grand Cru
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.2.explanati: Grand Cru vineyards are subject to the strictest yield limits in Burgundy: 35–37 hl/ha for reds and slightly higher for whites. By comparison, regional Bourgogne permits up to 55 hl/ha. These low limits help ensure concentration and quality.
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.3.question: Which of the following does NOT have any Grand Cru vineyards?
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.3.explanati: The Côte Chalonnaise (including Mercurey, Givry, Rully and Montagny) has no Grand Cru vineyards — its highest classification is Premier Cru. All 33 Grands Crus are found in Chablis (7), the Côte de Nuits (24) and the Côte de Beaune (8).
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.4.question: How does a Burgundy Grand Cru fundamentally differ from a Bordeaux Grand Cru Classé?
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.4.options.0: A. Burgundy Grands Crus are older designations
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.4.options.1: B. Burgundy Grand Cru is awarded to a specific vineyard parcel; Bordeaux Grand Cru Classé is awarded to a specific estate (château)
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.4.options.2: C. Burgundy Grands Crus are more affordable
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.4.options.3: D. Burgundy Grand Cru is evaluated by the same criteria as Bordeaux
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.4.explanati: This is the fundamental philosophical difference: Burgundy Grand Cru belongs to the land — a specific, legally defined vineyard parcel whose character is paramount. In Bordeaux, Grand Cru Classé is a status awarded to an estate (château), meaning the building, infrastructure and brand are the basis of the classification.
lessons.0.slides.6.title: Summary
lessons.0.slides.6.content: Burgundy's 33 Grands Crus are the world's most precise demonstration of terroir-based quality classification — a system built on centuries of observation and confirmed by the consistent excellence these 566 hectares produce when farmed and vinified with care.
lessons.1.title: Côte de Nuits Grands Crus (24 Parcels)
lessons.1.slides.0.title: Côte de Nuits Grands Crus (24 Parcels)
lessons.1.slides.0.subtitle: 20 minutes
lessons.1.slides.0.description: A complete survey of the 24 Grands Crus stretching from Gevrey-Chambertin to Vosne-Romanée — each one a unique expression of Pinot Noir.
lessons.1.slides.1.title: Gevrey-Chambertin: 9 Grands Crus
lessons.1.slides.1.content: More Grands Crus than any other village — powerful, structured and long-lived.
lessons.1.slides.1.keyPoints.0: Chambertin (12.9 ha): Napoleon's wine; the most powerful Grand Cru — dark fruit, iron and spice; ages 15–30 years
lessons.1.slides.1.keyPoints.1: Chambertin-Clos de Bèze (15.4 ha): may be labelled 'Chambertin'; similar power with slightly more elegance
lessons.1.slides.1.keyPoints.2: Charmes-Chambertin (31.1 ha): the largest, most approachable; soft and seductive; ages 8–20 years
lessons.1.slides.1.keyPoints.3: Mazoyères-Chambertin (18.3 ha): may use the Charmes-Chambertin label
lessons.1.slides.1.keyPoints.4: Chapelle, Griotte, Latricières, Mazis, Ruchottes-Chambertin: each 2.7–9.1 ha; distinct styles; ages 8–25 years
lessons.1.slides.2.title: Morey-Saint-Denis: 5 Grands Crus
lessons.1.slides.2.content: Balanced between Gevrey's power and Chambolle's elegance — arguably the most undervalued Grand Cru village.
lessons.1.slides.2.keyPoints.0: Clos de la Roche (16.9 ha): the largest and most powerful of Morey's Grands Crus
lessons.1.slides.2.keyPoints.1: Clos Saint-Denis (6.6 ha): the most elegant — this village lent its name to Morey
lessons.1.slides.2.keyPoints.2: Clos des Lambrays (8.7 ha): almost a monopole (one owner: Clos des Lambrays estate)
lessons.1.slides.2.keyPoints.3: Clos de Tart (7.5 ha): monopole of Mommessin (acquired by Pinault group, 2017)
lessons.1.slides.2.keyPoints.4: Bonnes-Mares: most of this Grand Cru is in Chambolle (but 1.5 ha lies in Morey)
lessons.1.slides.3.title: Chambolle-Musigny: 2 Grands Crus
lessons.1.slides.3.content: The most feminine, silken and floral village in all of Burgundy — its two Grands Crus represent opposite poles of elegance and power.
lessons.1.slides.3.keyPoints.0: Musigny (10.9 ha): the quintessence of Burgundy red wine — rose, violet, silken texture, endless persistence
lessons.1.slides.3.keyPoints.1: Musigny also produces a tiny amount of white (Musigny Blanc) — extraordinarily rare and expensive
lessons.1.slides.3.keyPoints.2: Bonnes-Mares (13.5 ha, mostly in Chambolle): more powerful and structured than Musigny; ages 15–25 years
lessons.1.slides.3.keyPoints.3: Musigny: Domaine Comte Georges de Vogüé holds the largest share (72% of Musigny)
lessons.1.slides.4.title: Vougeot, Vosne-Romanée and Flagey Grands Crus
lessons.1.slides.4.content: The southern heartland — including the world's most expensive wine.
lessons.1.slides.4.keyPoints.0: Clos de Vougeot (50.6 ha): Burgundy's largest red Grand Cru; 80+ owners; quality varies enormously by parcel
lessons.1.slides.4.keyPoints.1: Romanée-Conti (1.81 ha): DRC monopole; the world's most expensive wine — €15,000–50,000+ per bottle
lessons.1.slides.4.keyPoints.2: La Tâche (6.06 ha): DRC monopole; power and elegance combined
lessons.1.slides.4.keyPoints.3: Richebourg (8.03 ha), Romanée-Saint-Vivant (9.44 ha), La Romanée (0.85 ha, smallest Grand Cru)
lessons.1.slides.4.keyPoints.4: Échézeaux (37.7 ha) + Grands Échézeaux (9.1 ha) in Flagey — technically their own commune
lessons.1.slides.5.title: 💡 Key Take-aways
lessons.1.slides.5.points.0: 🍷 Gevrey-Chambertin (9 Grands Crus) = power and depth; Chambolle-Musigny (2) = elegance and floral silk
lessons.1.slides.5.points.1: 🍷 Morey-Saint-Denis has 5 Grands Crus but receives less recognition — outstanding value for Grand Cru quality
lessons.1.slides.5.points.2: 🍷 DRC dominates Vosne-Romanée: Romanée-Conti and La Tâche are both DRC monopoles
lessons.1.slides.5.points.3: 🍷 Clos de Vougeot's fragmented ownership (80+ owners) means producer selection is as critical as vineyard name
lessons.1.slides.6.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.0.question: Which is the only Côte de Nuits Grand Cru that also produces a Grand Cru white wine?
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.0.explanati: Musigny is unique in the Côte de Nuits — it produces primarily Grand Cru red Pinot Noir, but also a tiny amount (less than 0.6 ha under Domaine Comte de Vogüé) of Grand Cru white Chardonnay (Musigny Blanc). It is extraordinarily rare — fewer than 500 cases are produced per year.
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.1.question: What makes Clos de Vougeot particularly unusual as a Grand Cru?
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.1.options.0: A. It is the only Grand Cru in Vougeot village
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.1.options.1: B. It is the world's oldest vineyard
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.1.options.2: C. At 50.6 ha it is Burgundy's largest red Grand Cru, shared by more than 80 different owners
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.1.options.3: D. It produces only white wine
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.1.explanati: Clos de Vougeot is unique for its scale (50.6 ha) and extreme fragmentation (80+ owners). Wine quality varies enormously from the top of the slope (elegant, complex) to the bottom (less distinguished). The producer's identity is arguably more important than the vineyard name for this Grand Cru.
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.2.question: What is the area of Romanée-Conti, and who owns it?
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.2.options.1: B. 1.81 ha, exclusive monopole of Domaine de la Romanée-Conti (DRC)
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.2.options.2: C. 12 ha, the largest Grand Cru in Vosne-Romanée
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.2.options.3: D. 0.5 ha, owned by the Leroy family
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.2.explanati: Romanée-Conti covers exactly 1.81 ha and is a total monopole — exclusively owned and produced by Domaine de la Romanée-Conti. Its tiny production (approximately 450–500 cases per year) and legendary quality make it consistently the world's most expensive wine.
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.3.question: Which Morey-Saint-Denis Grand Cru is almost exclusively owned by a single estate (near-monopole)?
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.3.explanati: Clos des Lambrays (8.7 ha) is effectively a near-monopole — the vast majority is owned by the Clos des Lambrays estate, now owned by LVMH. (A tiny parcel belongs to another owner.) Clos de Tart is a true monopole (Mommessin/Pinault).
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.4.question: Chambertin-Clos de Bèze has a unique labelling privilege. What is it?
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.4.options.0: A. It may use the Gevrey-Chambertin Premier Cru label
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.4.options.1: B. It may be labelled as 'Chambertin' (using Chambertin's name), but Chambertin may not be labelled as Clos de Bèze
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.4.options.2: C. It can be labelled as both a red and a white wine
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.4.options.3: D. It shares the same legal production zone as Chambertin
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.4.explanati: By AOC rule, Chambertin-Clos de Bèze may optionally be labelled as 'Chambertin' (the more famous name), because Clos de Bèze historically predates Chambertin. However, the reverse is not permitted — a bottle labelled 'Chambertin' cannot come from the Clos de Bèze parcel unless it opts into the Chambertin designation.
lessons.1.slides.7.title: Summary
lessons.1.slides.7.content: The 24 Grands Crus of the Côte de Nuits span a stylistic arc from Gevrey-Chambertin's iron-fisted power to Vosne-Romanée's silk and spice — with Morey's intellectual complexity and Chambolle's floral elegance in between. Together they represent Pinot Noir at its absolute pinnacle.
lessons.2.title: Côte de Beaune and Chablis Grands Crus
lessons.2.slides.0.title: Côte de Beaune and Chablis Grands Crus
lessons.2.slides.0.subtitle: 15 minutes
lessons.2.slides.0.description: The white wine Grands Crus of the Côte de Beaune and Chablis — among the world's greatest expressions of Chardonnay.
lessons.2.slides.1.title: Côte de Beaune: Red Grand Cru — Corton
lessons.2.slides.1.content: Corton is the Côte de Beaune's only red Grand Cru, and at 97 ha the largest red Grand Cru in all of Burgundy — spanning three communes: Aloxe-Corton, Ladoix-Serrigny and Pernand-Vergelesses.
lessons.2.slides.1.keyPoints.0: Corton (97 ha total): multiple sub-parcels with different names (e.g. 'Corton-Bressandes', 'Corton-Clos du Roi')
lessons.2.slides.1.keyPoints.1: Style: powerful, more rustic than Côte de Nuits reds; ages 10–20 years
lessons.2.slides.1.keyPoints.2: The hill of Corton: a distinct geological landmark rising above the Côte de Beaune
lessons.2.slides.1.keyPoints.3: Key producers: Domaine de la Romanée-Conti (Corton), Louis Latour, Bouchard Père et Fils
lessons.2.slides.2.title: White Grands Crus: Corton-Charlemagne
lessons.2.slides.2.content: Corton-Charlemagne covers approximately 71 ha on the upper slopes of the Hill of Corton, where white limestone soils replaced the red marl of the lower Corton red.
lessons.2.slides.2.keyPoints.0: Size: ~71 ha; spread across Aloxe-Corton and Pernand-Vergelesses
lessons.2.slides.2.keyPoints.1: Style: rich, powerful white with hazelnut, butter and citrus; requires 5–15 years of aging
lessons.2.slides.2.keyPoints.2: Legend: the vineyard is named after Emperor Charlemagne, who reputedly preferred white wine to red
lessons.2.slides.2.keyPoints.3: Key producers: Coche-Dury (the most sought-after), Louis Latour, Bonneau du Martray
lessons.2.slides.3.title: The Montrachet Family of White Grands Crus
lessons.2.slides.3.content: The five Grands Crus of the Puligny-Montrachet / Chassagne-Montrachet zone represent the absolute pinnacle of white Burgundy — and arguably the world's greatest dry white wine zone.
lessons.2.slides.3.keyPoints.0: Le Montrachet (7.99 ha): the greatest white wine in the world according to many critics — shared between Puligny and Chassagne
lessons.2.slides.3.keyPoints.1: Chevalier-Montrachet (7.36 ha): above Le Montrachet; more mineral and precise
lessons.2.slides.3.keyPoints.2: Bâtard-Montrachet (11.86 ha): powerful and voluptuous; shared between Puligny and Chassagne
lessons.2.slides.3.keyPoints.3: Bienvenues-Bâtard-Montrachet (3.69 ha): lighter, elegant style in Puligny
lessons.2.slides.3.keyPoints.4: Criots-Bâtard-Montrachet (1.57 ha): smallest Grand Cru, entirely in Chassagne
lessons.2.slides.4.title: Chablis: 7 White Grands Crus
lessons.2.slides.4.content: Chablis's 7 Grands Crus cover approximately 100 ha of south-facing slopes on Kimmeridgian limestone — the geological foundation of Chablis's unique minerality.
lessons.2.slides.4.keyPoints.0: 7 Grands Crus: Blanchot, Bougros, Les Clos, Grenouilles, Les Preuses, Valmur, Vaudésir
lessons.2.slides.4.keyPoints.1: Total area: ~100 ha, all facing south or south-west on the right bank of the Serein river
lessons.2.slides.4.keyPoints.2: Les Clos (26 ha): the most powerful and structured; the 'Chambertin' of Chablis
lessons.2.slides.4.keyPoints.3: Vaudésir: elegant and mineral; Valmur: complex and rich; Grenouilles: floral and delicate
lessons.2.slides.4.keyPoints.4: Key producers: Raveneau, Dauvissat, Louis Michel, William Fèvre
lessons.2.slides.5.title: 💡 Key Take-aways
lessons.2.slides.5.points.0: 🍷 Corton is the only red Grand Cru in the Côte de Beaune — the others are white (or tiny Le Montrachet is the greatest dry white in the world)
lessons.2.slides.5.points.1: 🍷 Le Montrachet is described by many as the greatest dry white wine in the world
lessons.2.slides.5.points.2: 🍷 Chablis Grand Cru is a completely different style from Côte de Beaune whites — mineral, austere, exceptional
lessons.2.slides.5.points.3: 🍷 Corton-Charlemagne + Le Montrachet = the twin summits of Chardonnay in the Côte de Beaune
lessons.2.slides.6.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.0.question: Which is the ONLY red Grand Cru in the Côte de Beaune?
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.0.explanati: Corton is the only red Grand Cru in the Côte de Beaune. All others in this zone (Montrachet family, Corton-Charlemagne, Chablis Grands Crus) produce white wine. Musigny is in the Côte de Nuits.
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.1.question: What is the total area of Le Montrachet Grand Cru?
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.1.explanati: Le Montrachet covers exactly 7.99 ha, divided between the communes of Puligny-Montrachet and Chassagne-Montrachet. Despite its relatively modest size, it is considered by many critics to be the world's greatest site for dry white wine.
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.2.question: How many Grand Cru vineyards does Chablis have?
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.2.explanati: Chablis has exactly 7 Grand Cru vineyards: Blanchot, Bougros, Les Clos, Grenouilles, Les Preuses, Valmur and Vaudésir. They cover approximately 100 ha of south-facing Kimmeridgian limestone slopes on the right bank of the Serein river.
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.3.question: Which Chablis Grand Cru is considered the most powerful and structured?
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.3.explanati: Les Clos (26 ha, the largest Chablis Grand Cru) is consistently described as the most powerful and age-worthy of the seven — the 'Chambertin' of Chablis. It produces wines of exceptional minerality, structure and longevity, needing 8–15 years to fully express themselves.
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.4.question: What famous person gave his name to Corton-Charlemagne?
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.4.options.2: C. Philip the Bold (Duke of Burgundy)
lessons.2.slides.6.questions.4.explanati: Corton-Charlemagne is named after the Emperor Charlemagne (742–814), who according to legend owned vineyards on the Hill of Corton. His wife allegedly persuaded him to plant white grapes on the upper slopes to prevent red wine staining his white beard — though this charming story is likely apocryphal.
lessons.2.slides.7.title: Summary
lessons.2.slides.7.content: The white Grands Crus of the Côte de Beaune (Montrachet family, Corton-Charlemagne) and Chablis represent the world's most authoritative benchmark for Chardonnay — each with its own irreducible identity, from the opulent richness of Le Montrachet to the mineral austerity of Les Clos.
